nameStory: The 'black' in black highbush blueberry comes from its distinctively dark-colored berries, which lack the silvery-blue coating (called a glaucous bloom) found on regular blueberries. The 'highbush' part distinguishes it from its low-growing cousins that hug the ground, as this species grows tall enough that you can pick berries without bending over much.
description: Black highbush blueberry is an upright deciduous shrub that can grow several feet tall, making it one of the taller blueberry species in New England. Unlike the familiar blueberries you might know, this species produces distinctively dark, almost black berries without the typical silvery coating. The entire plant has a somewhat fuzzy appearance due to fine hairs covering the stems and undersides of leaves, giving it a softer texture than other blueberries. It's a member of the heath family, related to cranberries, azaleas, and rhododendrons.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Berries are distinctively dark purple to black without the silvery-blue coating typical of other blueberries - they look almost like tiny grapes when ripe

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Undersides of leaves feel noticeably fuzzy due to fine, somewhat dingy-colored hairs that give them a soft, velvety texture

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Young twigs and branches are covered in fine hairs, making them feel slightly fuzzy to the touch rather than smooth

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, bell-shaped white to pinkish flowers appear very early in spring, often before many other blueberries bloom

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as an upright, multi-stemmed shrub that can reach eye level or taller, with a somewhat open, airy appearance

habitat: Black highbush blueberry thrives in New England's wettest places - look for it in bogs, swamps, and marshy areas where the soil stays consistently moist. It's particularly fond of acidic, peaty soils and can often be found growing alongside other bog plants like cranberries, sphagnum moss, and pitcher plants. You might spot it around the edges of ponds or in low-lying areas that flood seasonally.

seasonality.spring: Very early white to pale pink bell-shaped flowers appear before most other blueberries bloom, often while nights are still chilly. New leaves emerge with a fresh green color and soft, fuzzy texture.
seasonality.summer: Dark purple to black berries ripen in mid to late summer, standing out dramatically against the green foliage. The fuzzy leaf undersides become more noticeable as the plant reaches full size.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn brilliant shades of red, orange, and yellow, creating stunning autumn displays in wetland areas. The fuzzy stems become more visible as leaves drop.
seasonality.winter: Bare fuzzy twigs and reddish-brown bark help identify the plant, along with any persistent dried berries that birds may have missed.

funFact: Black highbush blueberry berries are so dark they were traditionally used by Native Americans as a natural dye for baskets and clothing, creating rich purple and black colors that could last for years.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with northern highbush blueberry, but remember: if the berries look like tiny black grapes without any silvery coating and the stems feel fuzzy, you've found the black highbush. Regular highbush blueberries have that characteristic silvery-blue bloom on their berries and smooth stems.
contextualKnowledge: Some botanists consider black highbush blueberry to be just a variety of northern highbush blueberry rather than a separate species, so you might see it listed differently in various field guides. The scientific debate doesn't change what you'll see in the field - the distinctive dark berries and fuzzy stems make it easy to recognize regardless of how it's classified.
compareHints: Among New England's blueberries, black highbush stands out for its distinctively dark berries and fuzzy stems and leaves. Lowbush blueberries grow much shorter and have smooth stems, while northern highbush blueberry has the typical silvery-blue berries and lacks the fuzzy texture. The early blooming time also helps separate it from most of its Vaccinium relatives, which tend to flower later in spring.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its Vaccinium cousins, lingonberry is evergreen while blueberries lose their leaves in winter.
Differs from highbush blueberry mainly by size - lowbush stays under 2 feet while highbush can reach 6-12 feet tall.
American cranberry is much more robust than its cousin bog cranberry, with leaves twice the size and significantly larger berries.
Unlike lowbush blueberry which has green leaf undersides and toothed leaf edges, bog bilberry has distinctly pale leaf undersides and smooth-edged leaves.
Among its Vaccinium relatives, northern highbush blueberry is easily the tallest – lowbush blueberry stays under 2 feet, while lingonberry and the various cranberries are ground-hugging plants.
Among New England blueberries, velvetleaf blueberry is the only one with distinctly fuzzy leaves - lowbush and highbush blueberries have smooth, hairless leaves.

Among its Vaccinium relatives, bog cranberry is distinguished by its extremely small size and creeping habit - while lowbush blueberries also stay low, they form upright clumps rather than trailing mats.
Unlike highbush blueberries that grow tall and upright, early lowbush stays under 3 feet and spreads horizontally.
Unlike lowbush and highbush blueberries which have stamens that stay tucked inside their flowers, deerberry's stamens prominently stick out like tiny antennae.
Unlike its lowland cousins like lowbush blueberry and highbush blueberry, dwarf bilberry stays extremely small and produces single berries instead of clusters.
Compared to lowbush blueberry, northern blueberry prefers cooler climates and higher elevations, with slightly rounder leaves and often more intense berry flavor.
